title: State v. Mustak Hussain
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Convicted u/s 135; civil liability settled and deposited during trial; posted for sentence
statutes: Third proviso to Section 135(1) Electricity Act 2003

interpretations.interpretation: A long cable hooked from the licensee's pole to run scrap work at unmetered premises is a clause (a) connection with the licensee's lines. 'Dishonestly' takes its s.24 IPC meaning (wrongful gain/wrongful loss).

Reverse-onus clause: proof of an artificial/unauthorised means raises a compulsory presumption of dishonest use (Neeraj Dutt) rebuttable on the prudent-man standard (Hiten P. Dalal); natural rebuttal is paid bills / lawful metered use, the s.106 Evidence Act onus on the consumer (Mukesh Rastogi).

Inspection power with photo-ID safeguards (60); contemporaneous report, seizure/sealing, photo/video documentation (61); prosecution only where dishonest intention evident + 24-hour police complaint + missing-seal caution (62); assessment at twice tariff up to 12 months with credit for paid units (63). Unchallenged compliance confirms regularity; the Rs. 72,006 assessment measures the theft.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity to the accused.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.point: A worker's statement can anchor occupancy and theft
significance.explanation: The worker Sameer's statement placed the scrap work and the theft at the accused's premises; the accused never denied Sameer was his worker there.

significance.point: Silence on the advisory notice cuts against the accused
significance.explanation: The advisory notice invited a written objection within four working days; filing none was read as conduct consistent with guilt.

significance.point: Load size does not gate the offence
significance.explanation: A modest 1.501 KW load was still direct theft; the deliberately laid 14-metre cable showed an engineered, dishonest tap.
Settling and depositing the theft bill was read as conduct inconsistent with innocence.

significance.point: The reverse-onus presumption did the rest
significance.explanation: No meter, unexplained running load, no Genset, no paid bills — the compulsory presumption convicted.

generic_facts.theft_mode: direct theft — 14 m yellow cable hooked from licensee pole
generic_facts.premises: ground floor used for scrap work
generic_facts.ownership_evidence: ownership documents seized; worker's statement (s.161) recorded
generic_facts.defence: bare denial/false implication; no defence evidence; settled + deposited theft bill
